channel.title: Personal News Feed — News & World Affairs
channel.description: Personally scored news, world affairs, opinion/analysis & foreign affairs, business & finance, and San Diego/local articles curated by news-filter

item.title: Inflation Drives Consumers to Trade Down and Seek Value
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Original headline: Inflation is pushing consumers to trade down and hunt for value
Inflation is driving consumers to trade down and prioritize value, according to a Bank of America Institute report. The study analyzed spending trends across apparel, dining, grocery, and travel, showing a shift toward value-tier merchants since 2021. Economists note affordability pressures from rising gas prices, mortgage rates, and stagnant wage growth are forcing households to cut discretionary spending. Millennials, facing higher housing and childcare costs, are particularly affected, while Gen Z has lower spending power. Travel spending shows mixed trends, with hotel and cruise growth offsetting declines in airline transactions. University of Michigan surveys found 57% of consumers report eroded living standards due to high prices. Company executives highlighted value-conscious behavior, with higher-income shoppers seeking deals and lower-income households delaying non-essential purchases. Bank of America data shows wage growth remains positive but may not offset inflation's impact on essentials like housing.

item.title: Chula Vista university task force makes first recommendation, holds off on financing plan
item.description:
Source: San Diego Union-Tribune
The South County Higher Education Planning Task Force recommended state lawmakers continue working with Chula Vista to draft legislation shielding a proposed $2.17 billion university district from California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) challenges. The motion, backed by members Adrian Arancibia and Valita Jones, passed without opposition. The task force, created by Assemblymember David Alvarez’s AB662, must submit governance, financing, and land-use recommendations by July 1. Members deferred financing decisions until January, citing unresolved legal issues. Adriana Ochoa, the task force’s legal counsel, noted deadlines to challenge the 2018 environmental impact report have passed, but future approvals like permits could still face litigation. Ochoa also proposed amending the Surplus Land Act exemption to require 50% market-rate housing, as student and staff units cannot be designated affordable. Assembly Bill 76, aimed at addressing the issue, was vetoed as premature. Member Gala Ledezma questioned whether the requirement genuinely blocks development. Nicole Salazar of PFM Financial Advisors noted no comparable examples of a 50% market-rate threshold. The task force outlined next steps including forming a joint powers authority, seeking state funding, and advancing pre-development planning. Chair Clarissa Reyes Falcon said the task force will return in January with a full package addressing governance, financing, and the Surplus Land Act. The next meeting is scheduled for January 22.

item.title: San Diego Weather Causes Flight Delays and Event Disruptions
item.description:
Source: ABC 10News San Diego Original headline: Friday's wet weather causes flight delays, impacts events around the San Diego area
Wet weather caused flight delays and disrupted events in San Diego Friday. San Diego airport implemented a ground delay starting around 7:30 a.m., with departures averaging half-hour delays. The airport reported nearly 80 departure delays and two cancellations, plus over 80 arrival delays and two cancellations. The Susan G. Komen 3-Day event faced delays as overturned tables and tents forced organizers to delay the event amid cleanup. Isolated showers continued through the day, with a second storm expected to increase shower activity overnight into Saturday. Light showers possible Saturday, with Sunday forecasted to be mostly dry. Meteorologists noted lighter showers during the day on Saturday.

item.title: San Diego County reports rising mpox cases, expands vaccine outreach
item.description:
Source: San Diego Union-Tribune Original headline: Mpox cases rise, prompting expanded county public health outreach
San Diego County reported 16 mpox cases since October, raising the annual total to 48, up from 35 in 2025. The virus, transmitted through close contact, has two variants: Clade II, which caused most cases since 2022, and Clade I, which circulated in California since 2025. Officials confirmed 10 Clade I cases since July 2026. Of the recent cases, 10 involved unvaccinated individuals. The JYNNEOS vaccine, which protects against both variants, is recommended. California’s Department of Public Health linked Clade I’s rise to returning travelers from Europe, with recent cases tied to state travel. San Diego County increased case reporting frequency to weekly. Dr. Ankita Kadakia urged vaccination, noting the vaccine prevents severe illness. Mpox, which causes rash, fever, and fatigue, has been present since 2022, peaking at 469 cases. Vaccines are available at Sexual Health Clinics.

item.title: Mortgage Rates Rise to 7.26% on Friday, November 13
item.description:
Source: NerdWallet Original headline: Mortgage Rates Today, Friday, November 13: Kind of a Big Jump
Mortgage rates surged to 7.26% APR on Friday, November 13, up 17 basis points from the prior day and 28 basis points from a week ago. The increase follows mixed Producer Price Index data showing 0.3% monthly inflation, below forecasts, but 6.5% year-over-year growth—the highest in four years. Analysts expect the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates again in December, which typically drives up mortgage rates. Borrowers are advised to consider refinancing if current rates are at least 0.5 to 0.75 percentage points lower than existing rates, though affordability and long-term goals should guide decisions. Lenders adjust rates frequently, so locking in a rate may be prudent. Personalized quotes vary based on credit scores, down payments, and other financial factors, making it unlikely to secure the advertised rate without a lock. Consumers are urged to assess their ability to afford payments at current rates before proceeding with a mortgage application.

item.title: FAA Orders U.S. Flight Grounding Amid Communication Crisis
item.description:
Source: San Diego Union-Tribune Original headline: Cancelación de vuelos en EE.UU. afecta al Aeropuerto Internacional de San Diego
The FAA ordered all U.S. flights to be grounded due to a communication issue affecting air traffic control centers. At San Diego International Airport, all aircraft remained on the ground Friday, though landings were permitted. The FAA’s directive stated that 'all air operations are grounded by order of the Federal Aviation Command Center' pending resolution of the problem. U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy confirmed the FAA’s decision, citing a 'communication problem' impacting all control centers. Travelers faced uncertainty, with Daniel Hong, a Vancouver resident, waiting for Air Canada updates after arriving at the airport unaware of the cancellation. Brenna Hilbert, celebrating her 40th birthday in San Diego, described the situation as 'uncontrollable' after her Frontier Airlines flight was delayed multiple times. International flights were managed on a case-by-case basis. Airport officials noted many travelers had already checked flight status and postponed arrivals. The grounding occurred on Friday the 13th, adding to the disruption.

item.title: SpaceX Starship Test Flight Ends in Booster Explosion
item.description:
Source: BBC News, Deutsche Welle Original headline: SpaceX Attempts Starship Rocket Recovery Amid Test Flight Challenges
SpaceX attempted to recover the Starship rocket's lower stage during a test flight but failed, with the booster diverting to the Gulf of Mexico and exploding. The 124-meter rocket launched successfully from Texas, carrying the upper stage to orbit to deploy 26 Starlink satellites. The lower stage, or Super Heavy booster, was intended to be caught by mechanical arms on the launch tower six-and-a-half minutes after liftoff. Instead, it was redirected and crashed, according to a SpaceX spokesperson who cited safety as a priority. The upper stage, called the Ship, is set to return to Earth Saturday for a potential second recovery attempt. This marks the first full recovery attempt for Starship, a key step toward reusability and cost reduction. Previous tests had captured the booster but not the upper stage. The failure highlights ongoing challenges in achieving full reusability, a goal that could transform space economics. Malcolm Macdonald of the Royal Aeronautical Society noted that while one successful flight won’t prove the model, it could signal a shift toward operational testing. SpaceX faces scrutiny from shareholders and NASA, which relies on Starship for its 2028 lunar mission. Competitors like Blue Origin are also vying for NASA contracts. Despite the setback, SpaceX aims for weekly launches by 2027, as outlined by Elon Musk. The incident underscores the complexity of reusable rocket systems, a goal the company has pursued since 2015 with Falcon 9. Next steps focus on refining recovery processes and addressing technical hurdles to make spaceflight more affordable.

item.title: US Extends Medicaid Work Requirement Deadline to July
item.description:
Source: San Diego Union-Tribune Original headline: US gives states another 6 months before they have to remove people from Medicaid for not working
The Trump administration has delayed the nationwide Medicaid work requirement deadline to July 1, giving states more time to implement the policy. Originally set for January 1, the requirement mandates that beneficiaries work, volunteer, or attend school to retain coverage. States must determine eligibility based on work status by July, though they can choose not to remove beneficiaries until then. CMS acknowledged implementation challenges, with experts like Kathy Hempstead noting the delay will reduce coverage losses due to administrative errors. Democrats, gaining control of Congress, plan to roll back the requirement, citing concerns over medically frail individuals. A Boston court ruling exempted frail patients from the rule. Critics argue paperwork verification will be the main hurdle, as seen in Nebraska, where 533 people were denied coverage in May–August, mostly due to incomplete documentation. Amy Behnke of Nebraska’s Health Care Center Association warned that many eligible individuals may have lost coverage due to procedural issues.

item.title: Delivery Apps Depend on Small Group of Superusers, Data Shows
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Original headline: Apps like DoorDash or Uber Eats rely on a small group of superusers, new federal data shows
Delivery apps like DoorDash and Uber Eats rely on a small group of heavy users, according to new federal data. The Federal Reserve's 2025 Survey of Consumer Finances found that consumers in their mid-40s or younger who spend hundreds to thousands annually on food delivery are key to app revenue. Jeremy Horpedahl, an economics professor, noted these users are critical for retention. The survey revealed that 80% of respondents spent $0 on food delivery, suggesting many have never used such services. Top spenders, particularly those under 35, spent a median $1,800 annually, while those aged 35-44 spent $2,400. This contrasts with broader retail trends of declining spending, as DoorDash and Uber Eats continue to grow. The survey includes other delivery services and may miss one-time users. Horpedahl argued that capturing even a small percentage of these high-spending users could be lucrative for competitors. DoorDash expanded its platform and promoted DashPass to retain frequent users.

item.title: Three San Diego Burritos Ranked Among U.S. Best
item.description:
Source: San Diego Union-Tribune Original headline: 3 San Diego burritos named among America’s best in Beli app ranking
Beli, a social dining app, ranked the U.S.'s 12 best burritos, with three from San Diego making the list. La Perla Cocina Mexicana placed second, Mike’s Taco Club at fifth, and Ortiz’s Taco Shop in seventh. The top burrito came from La Azteca Tortilleria in Los Angeles. Rankings were based on reviews and ratings. Beli, founded in 2021, uses head-to-head comparisons instead of star ratings. Over 140 million ratings from 2 million users in 192 countries contributed to the list. All three San Diego entries specialize in California burritos, a high-carb dish with carne asada and french fries originating from a 1980s San Diego taco shop.

item.title: EU Holds First AI Summit Amid Chip Shortfalls and Global Tensions
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Original headline: The EU’s First AI Summit
European Union leaders convened in Dublin for the bloc’s first AI summit amid concerns over falling short of chip-manufacturing goals. The 2023 European Chips Act aimed to double the EU’s semiconductor production share to 20% by 2030, but the bloc remains behind the U.S. (53.73 gigawatts) and China (31.9 gigawatts) in data center capacity. European Council President António Costa emphasized AI’s importance, calling for responsible governance and global standards. The summit’s focus may be diverted by negotiations on Russia-Ukraine peace talks, with unclear EU representation. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation over alleged misconduct also drew attention. Meanwhile, Russia investigated assassination attempts targeting officials, with Ukraine accused of past attacks. Iran claimed to have destroyed a U.S. radar system in Bahrain, while the U.S. denied damage. U.S. President Trump shifted Vice President Vance’s focus from Iran to Democratic corruption investigations. The summit highlighted the EU’s struggle to compete globally in AI and semiconductors amid geopolitical tensions.

item.title: EU to Send Unified Team to Russia-Ukraine Peace Talks
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Original headline: Ukraine updates: Europe to send united front to potential peace talks
The EU has named representatives to attend potential peace talks between Russia and Ukraine. EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas stated Russia does not want 'anybody strong' at the negotiating table, while Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Russia wants to see 'genuineness' before allowing EU participation. European Council President Antonio Costa announced the EU will send a five-nation team including France, Germany, Italy, Poland, and the UK. Russia has rejected the idea of European involvement, with Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova denying discussions with US envoy Jared Kushner. The EU lacks consensus on representation, with Kallas claiming she represents Europe in foreign policy. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz urged US President Donald Trump to avoid 'surprises' during talks with Putin. Zelenskyy criticized Starshield internet issues, and Kyiv faces energy disruptions from Russian airstrikes. Russia insists on understanding Europe's 'real intentions' before expanding peace talks. US negotiators claimed Putin agreed to an EU seat, but Peskov said Russia has not yet decided.

item.title: Harbor Island Hotel Project Delayed Again After Decade-Long Effort
item.description:
Source: San Diego Union-Tribune Original headline: Plans for Harbor Island hotel delayed yet again following decade-long effort
Sunroad Enterprises and the Port of San Diego seek another two-year extension for the $200 million Harbor Island hotel project, now delayed for a decade. The Port’s Board of Commissioners will vote on an amendment to Sunroad’s lease agreement, extending the deadline to December 31, 2028, and requiring reimbursement if the Port builds a pedestrian path. Staff report cited rising construction costs, interest rates, and financing challenges as reasons for the delay. Sunroad first entered the option agreement in 2021, with construction originally due by year’s end. The project includes two hotels, amenities, and a public promenade. The Port previously granted $19 million in rent concessions to ease financing. Manchester Financial Group’s Ted Eldredge noted similar struggles in securing funding for a Fairmont hotel. Sunroad’s request follows prior delays, including issues with working drawings and project design. The California Coastal Commission previously blocked a smaller hotel project due to concerns over affordable lodging on tidelands. The Port’s approval hinges on addressing these ongoing challenges.

item.title: Unauthorized drones trigger security response at U.S. base in England
item.description:
Source: San Diego Union-Tribune Original headline: Drone activity over US base in Britain prompts security response, US military says
Unauthorized drone activity prompted a security response at U.S. Air Force Europe’s base at RAF Lakenheath in England. The U.S. military confirmed no personnel, aircraft, or infrastructure were affected. This incident marks the third U.S. base in the UK facing threats recently. Days earlier, over a dozen aircraft were moved from RAF Mildenhall due to a threat, prompting an elevation of the alert level to FPCON Charlie. A group of men was detained after suspicious vans were spotted near RAF Fairford, linked to Iran, leading to the withdrawal of U.S. bombers. Three men were charged with plotting to attack RAF Fairford. Separately, a U.S. Army officer at a NATO base near Gloucester was arrested for suspected Russian espionage, though officials said it was unrelated to the Iran-linked plot. The U.S. military emphasized collaboration with UK authorities to ensure security.

item.title: Germany Expands Intelligence Powers to Counter Hybrid Threats
item.description:
Source: BBC News, Deutsche Welle
Germany's parliament approved expanded intelligence powers for its foreign and domestic agencies to counter hybrid threats. The reforms, led by Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt, grant the Federal Intelligence Service (BND) and Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution (BfV) authority to conduct covert operations abroad, disrupt state-sponsored hacker groups, disable cyber-attack infrastructure, and sabotage weapons supply chains. BfV agents may now dismantle explosives, block data flows during cyberattacks, plant false information, and enter homes covertly with authorization. The law received 309 votes in favor, 190 against, and 71 abstentions. Critics, including Left Party security spokeswoman Clara Bünger, warned the measures risk blurring the line between intelligence and law enforcement, while SPD's Sonja Eichwede supported the reforms as essential for national security. The legislation includes an independent oversight board and follows incidents like the discovery of a faulty explosive device at Leipzig Airport, attributed to Russian involvement. Dobrindt denied creating a secret police, but opponents called the law a 'monster' that could revive authoritarian practices. The debate highlights tensions between modernizing security and preserving democratic safeguards.

item.title: FBI Disrupts North Korean Crypto Theft Scheme; Billions Stolen
item.description:
Source: LA Times Original headline: FBI disrupts crypto theft scheme by North Korean hacking group; billions stolen so far
FBI and DOJ disrupted a North Korean hacking group's cryptocurrency theft scheme, seizing over $400 million stolen over 18 months. The group used a social engineering campaign called FaceStealer, impersonating contacts via LinkedIn, Telegram, and other platforms to lure victims into video calls. Hackers secretly recorded victims and tricked them into installing malware under the guise of technical support. The stolen funds are used to fund North Korea's 'rogue regime and illicit weapons program,' according to Principal Deputy Assistant Atty. Gen. M. Scott Proctor. The FBI also seized 900 webcam videos of victims in the crypto and Web3 industries. Separately, a North Korean military group called TraderTraitor stole $6 billion from Binance on Oct. 29, with $2.7 million frozen and $1.2 billion approved for seizure. Federal authorities continue efforts to trace and recover stolen virtual assets, issuing a public alert about the FaceStealer campaign. Bill Essayli, top federal prosecutor for Los Angeles, stated the seizure demonstrates the U.S. will combat cybercrime funding rogue states.

item.title: Canadian Airports Manage Post-Ground Stop Flight Surge
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Original headline: Canadian airports have taken on extra planes and passengers as the outage chaos rippled north
Canadian airports are managing increased traffic and passenger volumes following the lifting of a nationwide ground stop. Toronto Pearson International Airport confirmed the FAA ended the ground stop around 8:30 p.m., but U.S. flight disruptions persist. The airport deployed additional staff and resources, including support teams in terminals and the U.S. departures area, while coordinating with airlines. NAV CANADA, which operates Canada's air traffic system, reported systems were functioning normally during the outage. Retired Delta Air Lines pilot Mark Stephens noted Canadian airports are handling diverted U.S. international flights, with displaced aircraft returning to gates. As of 10 p.m. Eastern time, nearly 7,000 flights were canceled or delayed within, to, or from the U.S., and 1,000 flights were diverted, with airports like Denver, Chicago, and Los Angeles accommodating extra aircraft.

item.title: Polar Vortex Weakens Unprecedentedly Early, Sparks Cold Snap Concerns
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Original headline: What's going on with the polar vortex?
The polar vortex has weakened unprecedentedly early this year, with winds reversing direction, according to European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecast scientists Tim Stockdale and Frederic Vitart. French meteorological agency Meteo-France called the event 'unprecedented,' warning it increases the risk of cold air outbreaks in densely populated regions of the Northern Hemisphere, including the U.S., Europe, and East Asia. The vortex, a ring of cold air about 10-50 km above the Arctic, influences the jet stream, which drives weather patterns. Disruptions, like sudden stratospheric warming, can weaken the vortex, causing it to split or shift. This year's disruption could lead to extreme cold, similar to the 2021 Great Texas Freeze, though the Met Office notes it doesn't guarantee freezing temperatures. El Nino, an ongoing strong warming event in the Pacific, may moderate impacts, but its effect is uncertain. Scientists also debate whether Arctic warming linked to climate change is increasing vortex disruptions, though the connection remains inconclusive.

item.title: Zelensky Says US Proposes Ukraine Cede Donbas for NATO Membership
item.description:
Source: BBC News Original headline: US has floated Ukraine ceding Donbas for Nato membership, Zelensky says
US negotiators suggested Ukraine withdraw forces from Donbas in exchange for NATO membership, according to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. Zelensky stated the proposal was raised for the first time during recent talks with US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff. He said Ukraine would consider a referendum if the offer included security guarantees, no military constraints, and rebuilding funds. Russia has rejected NATO membership for Ukraine, demanding territorial concessions and neutrality. Zelensky reiterated Ukraine’s refusal to cede sovereign territory, though ceding Donbas control would symbolically accept Russian occupation. Recent talks followed tensions over Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil facilities and US pressure to pause them. Zelensky also mentioned potential elections post-peace deal, though martial law suspends voting. The proposal marks a shift from earlier US claims that NATO membership was off the table.

item.title: U.S. Flu Season Begins Early, Intensifying in South and West
item.description:
Source: San Diego Union-Tribune Original headline: The US flu season is off to a very early start. It’s targeting the South and West now
The U.S. flu season has begun earlier than usual, with seven states reporting high flu activity, up from two the previous week. Louisiana is experiencing the most severe cases, driven by low vaccination rates, poverty, and healthcare access challenges. The CDC notes that over 3% of doctor visits last week were for flu-like illness, and mid-October hospitalization rates are the highest seen that early in autumn in over 15 years. The CDC estimates 2.6 million illnesses, 36,000 hospitalizations, and 2,100 deaths so far this season. States with high activity include California, Oregon, South Carolina, Tennessee, Texas, and Washington. Doctors warn of accelerated spread ahead of Thanksgiving travel. Dr. Fred Lopez urges vaccination, noting the current vaccine may still protect against a mutated H1N1 strain. Health officials emphasize the vaccine’s effectiveness is under review but stress no immediate cause for concern. Vaccination is recommended unless someone has active symptoms, as the vaccine guards against multiple strains.

item.title: Southern California faces rain, surf, and snow from incoming storms
item.description:
Source: LA Times Original headline: Rain, dangerous surf and snow could hit Southern California. Here's where and when storms are expected
Southern California faces rain, dangerous surf, and snow from an incoming storm series. Forecasters predict widespread rainfall starting Friday afternoon, with totals up to an inch by Saturday. Light rain is expected, but minor flood advisories are possible, particularly for Los Angeles County beaches. Flooding in Wilmington stranded five vehicles, including a semitruck, due to rain and high tides. Authorities warned of moderate to significant beach erosion and shallow flooding, urging caution near high tides. High surf advisories are in effect through Tuesday, with surf heights reaching 8-12 feet on west-facing shores and up to 18-25 feet on the Central Coast, risking damage to piers and roads. Coastal areas like Morro Bay and Pismo experienced warnings, with temporary beach closures and restrictions on access. Snow is expected in the eastern Sierra, with up to a foot near Mt. Whitney, causing hazardous travel conditions. The National Weather Service also warned of strong winds and potential power line damage. In Northern California, evacuation alerts were issued for low-lying areas due to hazardous surf. Santa Cruz closed beaches and the wharf, emphasizing the risks to swimmers and rescuers.

item.title: Dermatologists Say Morning Face Washing Not Necessary, Warn Against Harsh Ingredients
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Original headline: You don’t need to wash your face every morning — but if you do, watch out for these ingredients
Dermatologists say morning face washing isn't necessary, with some advising against it entirely. Dr. Tanya Kormelli notes that the 'twice a day' guideline is too general, and that skin type dictates cleansing frequency. Greasy skin may need more cleansing, while older adults or those with dry skin should avoid harsh soaps. Surfactants in cleansers can strip skin, especially for sensitive or dry skin. Dr. Sama Carley recommends reducing use of salicylic acid or benzoyl peroxide in winter or dry climates. Evening cleansing is emphasized to remove pollutants and makeup. Moisturizing with ceramides and hyaluronic acid is key, with affordable options like CeraVe and Vanicream praised. Prescription retinol or tretinoin may be used sparingly for acne. Dermatologists warn against over-reliance on expensive products, advocating simple, gentle routines.

item.title: Peoria police order evacuations after credible bomb threat at Illinois plant
item.description:
Source: ABC News: Top Stories Original headline: Peoria police urge evacuations after reported bomb threat at Illinois plant
Peoria police ordered evacuations after a bomb threat at BioUrja Renewables, formerly ADM, prompted a one-mile radius lockdown. Authorities confirmed a credible threat package was found and neutralized by bomb technicians by 9:12 p.m. Friday. The search for explosives continued into Saturday. Police Chief Brad Dixon stated the threat was real, not a hoax, emphasizing the package's credibility. Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker coordinated with local agencies, urging public compliance with safety directives. A country music concert by Jon Pardi was canceled due to proximity to the site. Residents and businesses within the area were instructed to avoid the zone until further notice. Most streets remained closed as emergency personnel conducted a thorough inspection of the facility.

item.title: Pope Leo Celebrates Mass in Former Diocese of Chiclayo, Peru
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Original headline: Pope Leo celebrates Mass in his former diocese of Chiclayo, Peru
Pope Leo XIV celebrated an outdoor Mass in Chiclayo, Peru, his former diocese, where he served as bishop from 2015 to 2023. The Vatican estimates 1.5 million people attended despite 31°C heat, marking the centerpiece of his 12-day South American tour. Locals still refer to him as 'Padre Roberto' and 'amigo,' reflecting his deep ties to Peru, where he worked as a missionary for two decades. The pope, who holds Peruvian citizenship, arrived from Lima in a plane decorated with 'Leo XIV flies home' stickers. During his homily, he expressed gratitude for the crowd's prayers, particularly for his health during his lung cancer treatment. He will later speak at St. Turibius de Mogrovejo Catholic University, named after a 16th-century missionary he admired for advocating indigenous rights. The event followed record crowds in Uruguay and Argentina, with the largest gathering in Lima, where 3.5 million attended.

item.title: Mechanic Identified as Victim of Trailer Collapse
item.description:
Source: San Diego Union-Tribune Original headline: Mechanic crushed to death under semi-truck trailer identified
A mechanic identified as Raul Martinez Reyes, 64, was killed when a semi-truck trailer collapsed on him at a lot near Otay Mesa. Martinez was found pinned under the 53-foot trailer shortly after 10 a.m. Thursday, according to Cal Fire and the Medical Examiner’s Office. He died from multiple blunt-force injuries at the scene. The trailer was attached to a tripod when it fell, and Martinez was working on it at the time. Cal/OSHA is investigating the workplace incident. Martinez was a contract worker, not directly employed by Amazon, as confirmed by an Amazon spokesperson. County officials did not provide his city of residence. The Medical Examiner’s Office confirmed his identification.

item.title: San Diego Police Operation Aims to Reduce Gaslamp Quarter Violence
item.description:
Source: San Diego Union-Tribune Original headline: El Gaslamp Quarter se volvió un lugar alborotado. Una ofensiva policial ha intentado hacerlo más seguro. ¿Ha funcionado?
San Diego police launched Operation Last Call in late August to address violence and disorder in the Gaslamp Quarter. Resident Phillip Garcia reported feeling safer with increased police presence, including bike officers, during weekend nights. Authorities noted a 33% drop in violent crimes in October compared to 2024, with 168 arrests, 179 citations, and four weapons recovered in the first two months. During Halloween, officers handled 50 citations and five serious crimes, including a firearm seizure. Despite efforts, overcrowding, alcohol-related incidents, and unresolved tensions persist. Police chief Scott Wahl called the operation necessary to curb rising violence and disrespect for laws. Critics argue the problem shifts rather than diminishes, with some businesses and residents noting that crowds and altercations continue into later hours. Officer Colin Steinbroner emphasized coordination with medical teams to address intoxication cases. The area saw 345 violent incidents and two homicides in 2024, with police warning against drawing conclusions from viral videos. The operation added 25 officers, including bike units, to manage crowds and rapid response.

item.title: DHS Secretary Mullin: No U.S. Threat Amid FAA Ground Stop
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: News Original headline: DHS head Markwayne Mullin says there is not a threat to the U.S. amid FAA ground stop
DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin confirmed there is no threat to the U.S. amid a FAA-ordered ground stop. The FAA halted all flights due to communication difficulties, with Mullin stating the situation stems from a telecommunications outage, not a security threat. He emphasized that no nefarious attack was indicated and reassured travelers that all flights are accounted for. Mullin noted the outage is not linked to the FAA’s recent AI air traffic system or a Microsoft outage. Details about affected regions remain unclear, though two U.S. locations were unaffected. Officials are working to restore communications but provided no timeline for resolving the issue. International flights are being handled on a case-by-case basis, complicating efforts to land stranded aircraft. President Trump has not commented, though he is scheduled to travel to Asia next week. Travelers face uncertainty as airports grapple with grounding flights and managing incoming aircraft.

item.title: Stone Brewing's Escondido bistro closes after rebrand plans
item.description:
Source: ABC 10News San Diego Original headline: Stone Brewing's Escondido bistro closes its doors as founders plan a new rebrand
Stone Brewing's World Bistro and Gardens in Escondido closed permanently on Nov. 13 after serving as a flagship location. Founders Greg Koch and Steve Wagner plan to reopen the site under a new brand name, separate from Stone Brewing. Customers gathered to reflect on the venue's legacy, with many sharing personal memories. Glenn Wichert praised the bistro's atmosphere and expressed excitement for the future. Greg Koch described the space as his favorite, highlighting the lively energy of the dining area. Erik and Kelly Nelson recalled using the venue for their wedding rehearsal dinner and family events. Eric Kessler noted the emotional significance of the final day, including filling growlers and walking through the gardens. The closure marks the end of an era for the Escondido location, which had been a community staple for years.

item.title: Scientists test Alzheimer's prevention with early drug trials
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Original headline: What if we could stop Alzheimer's before it ever starts?
Maritza Ciliberto, 57, has been receiving an experimental Alzheimer's drug every two weeks for over a decade to prevent the inherited disease that killed her family members. The treatment, administered intravenously, carries risks like brain bleeding but aims to clear amyloid plaques before symptoms appear. Ciliberto is part of a clinical trial led by Dr. Randall Bateman at Washington University, where early results suggest starting treatment earlier may delay dementia onset. Researchers are shifting focus from treating Alzheimer's after symptoms emerge to preventing it by targeting amyloid buildup. New trials by Eli Lilly and Eisai are testing preventive use of amyloid-clearing drugs in people with no dementia but elevated brain amyloid levels. While some experts, like Dr. Bateman, see promise in early intervention, others like Richard Isaacson remain skeptical, noting that amyloid presence doesn't guarantee dementia. Ciliberto, who now pursues a master's degree and ministry, believes the treatment is working, while others like Jake Heinrichs have restructured their lives around the therapy. The research could redefine Alzheimer's as a manageable condition rather than an inevitable decline, though results from upcoming 2027-2028 trials will determine its viability.
